subject: math

objective.text: Solve word problems using decimal operations.

explanations.title: Draw it, then calculate
explanations.text: Draw a bar for the whole. Put the total on a bracket. Split the bar into equal parts. Put a question mark on the part you want.

explanations.title: Take out what is not shared first
explanations.text: In the Brandon problem some nuts were left out of the bags. Find the total, take away the leftover, then divide by the number of bags.

explanations.title: Two kinds of division
explanations.text: Sometimes the number of groups is known and you find the size of each group. Sometimes the group size is known and you find the number of groups.

questions.text: Divide 0.3 by 2.
Divide 0.9 by 5.
Divide 6.7 by 5.
Divide 0.58 by 4.
Divide 9.3 by 6.
Jesse and three friends buy trail mix for $5.42, apples for $2.55 and granola bars for $3.39. They split the cost equally among the four of them. How much should each friend pay?
Mr. Frye shares $126 equally among his 4 children for their weekly allowance. How much does each child get?
John pays his $31.50 allowance equally to his brother and two sisters. How much does each sibling get from John?
Each sibling already had $31.50 and gets $10.50 from John. How much does each sibling have in all?

source_ref.section: Concept Development Problem 1 (each sibling in all)

questions.text: Brandon mixes 6.83 pounds of cashews and 3.57 pounds of pistachios. What is the total weight in pounds?
Brandon has 10.4 pounds of nuts. He fills 6 same-size bags and has 0.35 pound left over. What does each bag weigh in pounds?
Lucas is 1.78 meters tall. Olivia is half as tall as Lucas. How tall is Olivia in centimeters?

source_ref.section: Exit Ticket and Problem Set (Exit Ticket 3, Olivia)

questions.text: Ava is 23 centimeters taller than Olivia. Olivia is 89 centimeters tall. How tall is Ava in centimeters?

source_ref.section: Exit Ticket and Problem Set (Exit Ticket 3, Ava)

questions.text: Mr. Hower can pay $510 down and then 8 monthly payments of $35.75. How much is that in all?

source_ref.section: Exit Ticket and Problem Set (Exit Ticket 4, payments)

questions.text: Paying cash for the computer costs $699.99. Paying in payments costs $796. How much does Mr. Hower save by paying cash?

source_ref.section: Exit Ticket and Problem Set (Exit Ticket 4, S: savings)

questions.text: A bakery buys 4 bags of flour that hold 3.5 kilograms each. A muffin batch needs 0.475 kilogram. A loaf of bread needs 0.65 kilogram. After 4 batches of muffins and 5 loaves of bread, how much flour is left in kilograms?

source_ref.section: Exit Ticket and Problem Set (Exit Ticket 5a)

questions.text: The bakery has 8.85 kilograms of flour left. Bins hold 3 kilograms each. How many bins are needed?

source_ref.section: Exit Ticket and Problem Set (Exit Ticket 5b)

questions.text: A gardener puts up 42.6 meters of fencing in a week. He does 13.45 meters on Monday and 9.5 meters on Tuesday. He does the rest in equal lengths on Wednesday to Friday. How many meters does he do each day?
Jenny charges $9.15 an hour for toddlers and $7.45 an hour for school-aged children. She babysits toddlers for 9 hours and school-aged children for 6 hours. How much does she earn in all?
Jenny wants to earn $1,300. She has earned $127.05. How much more does she need?
A table and 8 chairs weigh 235.68 pounds together. The table weighs 157.84 pounds. How much does one chair weigh in pounds?
Mrs. Cleaver mixes 1.24 liters of red paint with 3 times as much blue paint. She pours the blue paint equally into 5 containers. How much blue paint is in each container in liters?
How did the tape diagram in Problem 1a help you solve Problem 1b?
Some division problems find the size of each group. Others find the number of groups. Which is the Frye problem?
In the Brandon problem, why do you subtract the leftover nuts before you divide by 6?
How can a tape diagram show information in a story? Name two things you put on it.

hints.text: Draw the place value chart. Put each digit in its own place.
Multiplying by ten moves every digit one place to the left. Dividing moves it right.
Count the zeros in the number you multiply or divide by. That tells how many places the digits move.
The exponent tells how many tens are multiplied together. It matches the zeros.
Say the unit name. Then use a basic fact with that unit.
Think how many small units fit in a big unit. Then multiply or divide.
Add or subtract like units. Tenths with tenths, hundredths with hundredths.
Trade ten of a small unit for one of the next larger unit.
Compare digits from the left. Find the first place where they differ.
Rename both numbers with the same unit. Then compare.
Find the nearest numbers on each side for that place. Then check if you are past the halfway point.
Round the numbers and estimate first. Then place the decimal point.
Draw an area model. Multiply each unit by the whole number. Then add the partial products.
If you cannot share a unit evenly, trade it for ten of the next smaller unit.
Draw a tape diagram. Label the total and the parts.
Divide like whole numbers first. Then think about the unit to place the decimal point.
